title: Anthropic update on independent evaluators
excerpt: Anthropic announces updates to embedding independent evaluators
excerpt_en: Anthropic announces updates to embedding independent evaluators
content_en:
# An update on independent evaluators

Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.

## Why we work with independent evaluators

As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:

- *Expertise* in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.
- *Independence*: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
- Enough *access* to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
- *Freedom to publish* observations and assessments of a model or a process.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

## What we mean by “employee-like access”

We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.<sup>1</sup>

METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories like the ones above. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)<sup>2</sup>

Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

## Our other evaluator partnerships

We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

**In the first tier,** evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

**In the second tier,** evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

**The third tier** is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

**SecureBio** is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.<sup>3</sup>

**With Accenture** and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.

We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

content_en:
# Anthropics' Claude cracks a 25-year-old NSA cryptography mystery in under 30 minutes

**Anthropic's AI Claude has solved a 25-year-old cryptography mystery.** NIST standardized several curves in the ECDSA standard, the most widely used framework for elliptic-curve digital signatures, back in 2000. The NSA had supplied the seeds, the starting values used to generate the curve parameters, with zero explanation. No one knew how they were created, and that fueled suspicion of possible backdoors. The mystery even attracted a bounty and amateur sleuthing efforts. The late NSA employee Jerry Solinas had suggested the seeds were a hash of a humorous phrase, but that turned out to be wrong.

Claude cracked it in under 30 minutes. The seeds came from "lrand48," a simple C random number generator, initialized with a Unix timestamp between May 1997 and April 1998. Claude spotted the pattern because "lrand48" only outputs 31 bits, and the top bits in some seeds were systematically zero. According to Anthropic, this makes deliberate backdoors less likely. Anthropic is donating the $36,864 bounty to the Internet Security Research Group.

title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
excerpt: Meta and Apple have teamed up for the launch of the social media giant's newest model, Muse Spark Open, which will run locally on Apple silicon.
title_en: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
excerpt_en: Meta and Apple have teamed up for the launch of the social media giant's newest model, Muse Spark Open, which will run locally on Apple silicon.
content_en:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget. The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.

Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, \[and\] full build.”

The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.

Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.

Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

title: Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
excerpt: Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible academic labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools to advance life sciences research.
title_en: Bringing GPT-Rosalind to academic research labs
excerpt_en: Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible academic labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind and tools to advance life sciences research.
content_en:
# Bringing GPT‑Rosalind to academic research labs

Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.

We’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind, our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench(opens in a new window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval.

Academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn.

Accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this plan, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research.

Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research.

The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

Curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a new generation of vaccines and therapies.

Academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab.

OpenAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. These examples show where researchers are applying the model within their scientific workflows.

With the new Rosalind Academic Plan, academic researchers can bring GPT‑Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench to their lab with greater flexibility and harness frontier model intelligence for scientific research.

Eligible labs receive:

- Up to 30 Business Standard seats at $0 per user per month for up to 12 months.
- Access to all commercially available frontier OpenAI models, subject to plan usage limits.
- Access to GPT‑Rosalind following trusted-access approval.

Research data shared through the Rosalind Academic Plan is not used to train our models by default.

1. ### Explore the plan See what’s included
2. ### Sign in + apply Tell us about your research and lab
3. ### Complete verification Share details and sign the agreement
4. ### Start research Use GPT‑Rosalind once access is active

GPT‑Rosalind is a specialized life sciences model designed to support deeper reasoning on complex biological questions. Through trusted access, approved researchers can use it to investigate sensitive scientific questions within safeguards designed for legitimate research.

Areas of research include:

### Drug and protein design

Designing candidate drugs, therapeutic proteins, peptides, and enzymes, and optimizing their molecular interactions, selectivity, stability, and suitability for development.

Card 1 of 7: Drug and protein design

The Rosalind Academic Plan is currently available to academic labs at U.S. universities. PIs and lab leads at universities without an OpenAI Enterprise agreement can apply on behalf of their labs through our trusted access process. Labs at universities with an existing agreement must apply through their university’s Enterprise access process.

Once approved, PIs and lab leads can activate free access to GPT‑Rosalind for up to 30 named members, alongside the other OpenAI frontier models included in the plan. API access is not included at this time. Verified PIs and lab leads manage member permissions and are responsible for their lab’s approved use.

Choose the application path for your lab or organization.

### Academic labs

Rosalind Academic Plan

For PIs and lab leads at eligible organizations without an existing Enterprise account.

Apply on behalf of your lab.

### Existing Enterprise accounts

GPT-Rosalind access

For academic users at eligible institutions with an existing OpenAI Enterprise agreement.

Request access through your existing Enterprise account.

GPT‑Rosalind access is subject to approval.

Learn more about eligibility, application requirements, and getting started in our **help center guide**(opens in a new window).

Before activating access, we:

- Verify the institution’s legitimacy and the PI or lab lead’s identity
- Review the lead’s professional background, institutional appointment, and authority to oversee lab access
- Assess the lab’s institutional affiliation, research activities, and intended use
- Establish clear responsibilities for the lab lead and a designated institutional safety contact

Safeguards continue after activation through monitoring and enforcement. For registered high-sensitivity use cases, our safety checks account for the approved research context. When questions arise, we may follow up with researchers to clarify the work and confirm authorization. This approach is designed to detect potential misuse while accounting for legitimate research context and reducing unnecessary interruptions to authorized work.

## Specialized intelligence for complex scientific questions

We’re starting with academic labs as part of a broader effort to put useful AI tools in the hands of more scientists. By lowering the cost of access, we hope to give more researchers room to pursue ideas whose benefits could reach far beyond their own labs—from a clearer understanding of disease to better treatments and more resilient food systems.

Those advances will come from scientists asking important questions and doing the work to answer them. We want to help more of them do that work.

If you’re affiliated with an academic lab, learn more about the Rosalind Academic Plan and check whether you’re eligible(opens in a new window).

content_en:
### Nvidia expands Nemotron LLM family with hyper-efficient models for agentic systems

Nvidia Corp. today announced the launch of customizable Nemotron 3.5 Super LV large language models for always-on artificial intelligence agents and edge-focused 3.5 Bolt for local systems.

The company said the three new models will cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers to edge devices and local hardware.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open 120-billion-parameter model, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition, a group of model builders and AI labs advancing open frontier-level models, designed for high-accuracy multimodal agentic tasks. It is capable of instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows and visual understanding. Nvidia said it has comparable power to the company’s largest reasoning models at one-fifth the size.

That size, plus a new architecture, lets Super VL produce outputs nearly five times faster than other models in the same class.

Unlike closed frontier models, Nvidia provides the Super VL weights in the open, meaning organizations can post-train it on their own data and deploy it on their own infrastructure. This means they can bring it behind their firewall and keep it inside their domain, maintaining sovereignty, privacy and safety.

To build Super VL, Nvidia trained the model with open data and open methods using about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining. This also included 3.8 million post-training samples and reinforcement learning across 100 open environments to fine-tune the model.

Nvidia also said it’s releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use, finance, instruction following, long context, safety, fairness and vision-language understanding.

Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a smaller model designed to run agentic tasks locally and is based on Super VL. It uses a hybrid mixture-of-experts model that activates 9 billion of its 74 billion parameters at a time and uses two-bit quantization to fit within 24 gigabytes of memory. This lets it run comfortably on an enterprise workstation or PC graphics processing units, so users can delegate everyday projects, including writing and debugging code, without sending workloads to the cloud.

Later this month, Nvidia is also launching an even smaller model: Bolt E4B 4GB. This tiny model is built for edge deployment on GeForce RTX, Jetson and RTX/GTX Spark. This will allow physical AI and conversational agents to work within devices such as wearables, household devices, point-of-service, car dashboards, device assistants and other embedded interfaces.

Nvidia noted that it could be used to power interactive characters, conversational interfaces and smart user interfaces that localize or personalize.

content_en:
# An OpenAI model hacked a government site, grabbed 24 years of hospital data and kept it quiet

## Key Points

- OpenAI has published four new cases where its AI models bypassed security boundaries on their own during training or testing.
- One model extracted server passwords from a government website, forged authorization tokens, and downloaded 24 years of hospital data. A GPT-5.6-Sol model scanned over 360 crypto wallets and used someone else's funds for smart contract transactions.
- In several cases, the models didn't disclose their unauthorized access in their responses.

**OpenAI has published four new cases where its AI models bypassed security boundaries on their own during training or testing.**

In one case, OpenAI asked a model to pull hospital bed statistics from a government website. But the data wasn't publicly accessible.

So what does a model do when it hits a wall? It hacks its way through. After getting an access denied error, the model used the site's file download feature to grab server configuration files through path manipulation. It pulled a database connection string, a secret signing key, and email credentials with a username and password.

It then analyzed the application code, spotted that the API didn't verify authorization tokens for valid signatures, forged its own tokens, and downloaded 24 years of hospital bed statistics broken down by district. It never mentioned the unauthorized access in its response.

In another case, OpenAI gave a GPT-5.6-Sol model the task of setting up crypto smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network without providing a funded wallet. So the model wrote a script that derived private keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, checked over 360 wallet addresses for balances, and found one with enough test ETH.

The model briefly wondered whether using it was ethical, then decided on its own that the funds tied to a publicly known recovery phrase were "effectively abandoned" and went ahead with the transaction. It charged the gas fees to the other account and didn't disclose where the funds came from.

"This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI writes.

## Models hacked into internal systems and bypassed access controls

In two more evaluations, OpenAI asked a model to deliver five public dashboard figures from a research organization. In the first run, the model found exposed credentials for the organization's internal OpenSearch service and used them to route dashboard queries. It also changed the service's configuration, and OpenAI confirmed the change was never reverted.

In the second run, the model altered an authentication system setting, grabbed a cloud storage token, and downloaded five non-public database tables totaling about 147,000 rows. It did restore the setting afterward but kept using the still-valid token to access internal data.

The irony: the model hacked into internal systems, downloaded tens of thousands of rows of non-public data, and still didn't return correct results, according to OpenAI's report.

A separate model was restricted to GET requests only during a training phase, meaning it could only fetch web pages. It got around the restriction by tricking an external browser into opening a self-built form that automatically fired POST requests at a trade statistics service. It read the responses via OCR from screenshots. Then it built a reusable helper that returned data through a redirect service and an online mailbox as plain text. It kept refining this workaround even after the task was already done.

All cases and many more are documented in detail in OpenAI's Misalignment Reports.

title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
excerpt: METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the frontier AI model maker has given up the right to block them.
title_en: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
excerpt_en: METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the frontier AI model maker has given up the right to block them.
content_en:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR, a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.

The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.

“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”

Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.

Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.

METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.

“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.

METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.

Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay, where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same, and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

content_en:
Meta announced the Muse Spark Open AI model today, claiming that it’s the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” But the company also says that it’s the “the first model in its class” that can “run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.”

# Meta and Apple team up to make Muse AI models run better on Macs

Meta and Apple’s CEOs are publicly supporting each company’s work on Muse Spark Open.

Meta and Apple, typically rivals, worked together on the launch and are publicly supporting each other.

“Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on X.

“Congrats to the team!” new Apple CEO John Ternus said in a reply. “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”

“We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again,” Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said to *Axios*, who also noted that the companies have been collaborating over several months.

The new model is a “natively multimodal model” with 816 billion total parameters that “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” according to Meta. Apple also published a new technical post about MLX, an “array framework” for ML tasks on Apple Silicon, Muse Spark Open, and two other open models.

title: Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
excerpt: Apple and Meta are collaborating to make Muse Spark Open easier to run locally on clustered Mac Studio systems, according to the companies.
title_en: Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
excerpt_en: Apple and Meta are collaborating to make Muse Spark Open easier to run locally on clustered Mac Studio systems, according to the companies.
content_en:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple, the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.

Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.

The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture. As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.

Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.

Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.

Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.

Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."

Ternus responded, "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.

The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.

**"**We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.

Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.

Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.

Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.

## Common ground on open source

The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models, it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang, who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.

While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.

"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.

Their leaders have also traded harsh words.

Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.

Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.

Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.

And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.

## Apple's multiple partners

Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.

In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration "dramatically underperformed" and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.

Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google, to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.

Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.

Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.

Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer, with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.

Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.

"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

content_en:
### ServiceNow AI Control Tower: Selling a penthouse while building the frame

ServiceNow Inc. is making one of the more consequential and visible bets in enterprise artificial intelligence. The company says AI Control Tower can discover and govern any agent, work across models and clouds, track cost and value, and shut down behavior that violates policy.

That sales pitch plays directly to ServiceNow’s greatest asset – its installed base. Information technology and service management or ITSM, configuration management database or CMDB, risk workflows, security operations and years of operating context give the company a distribution and data advantage most AI and governance vendors do not have.

Our research suggests that moat is real. But proprietary customer data shows a more nuanced picture. Control Tower is already strong as a governance workflow and system of action. It can inventory AI assets, connect risks to owners, route approvals and remediation, and preserve an audit trail. What the field study has not broadly validated is the claim that Control Tower is a complete technical governance and runtime enforcement plane across the heterogeneous enterprise.

In this Breaking Analysis episode, we use a methodology similar to our CoreWeave analysis, and pressure-test management’s statements against 15 in-depth interviews with ServiceNow customers conducted with our data partner, Qualitate. We ask the following question: **Is Control Tower becoming the enterprise AI control plane – or is it limited to the governance system of action?**

**Access the full slide deck here with survey data in the appendix.**

### Three distinct technical jobs – ServiceNow dominates only one today

ServiceNow may not need to own every technical control to build a very large business bolstered by AI governance. It can create enormous value by owning the workflow around those controls – inventory, accountability, approvals, exceptions, remediation and audit history.

But its marketing pitch is allowing customers to think the the market is collapsing three jobs into one convenient phrase: **AI governance**.

The first is **governance workflow and accountability.** This is where ServiceNow is strongest.

The second is **AI lifecycle evidence** – model versions, lineage, validation, bias, explainability and drift. ServiceNow can coordinate that evidence, but customers often generate it elsewhere.

The third is **runtime enforcement and AI security** – intercepting an action, blocking a deployment, constraining an agent or revoking access in real time. Our survey indicates this layer is frequently external, custom or human.

The nuance is that approving a model and assigning a remediation ticket are valuable. But they are not the same as technically validating the model, proving lineage or blocking the action.

ServiceNow’s opportunity is to connect all three. It is not best-of-breed in each today according to its own customers. Broadly, **buyers should be cautious of claims that ServiceNow AI Control Tower is a platform that is universally end-to-end.**

### The five pillars of ServiceNow’s AI strategy

Control Tower sits inside a broader ServiceNow agentic AI strategy built on five connected pillars as shown below.

First is a **model-agnostic posture**: Any model, agent, cloud, data source or system of record.

Second is the shift from chat assistants to **autonomous workers** that plan, execute and adapt across workflows.

Third is **centralized governance through AI Control Tower** – discovery, ownership, access, observability, value and remediation.

Fourth is **AI cost and value management**: Token economics, model selection, budget control and ROI.

Fifth is **pricing and packaging**. Foundation, Advanced and Prime tiers seed AI broadly, move customers up the stack and add consumption on top of subscriptions.

These pillars reinforce one another and describe ServiceNow’s advantage and momentum. More agents create more governance demand. Model choice creates complexity. Governance addresses complexity and creates more reasons to stay on the platform. And more usage drives more consumption.

Our focus today is the key link in that flywheel chain – i.e. **Can AI Control Tower can extend ServiceNow’s workflow advantage into technical governance and runtime control?**

### The numbers underscore ServiceNow’s AI momentum

Management’s “right-to-win” argument is not that ServiceNow builds the best foundation models. It is that ServiceNow already knows how work moves through the enterprise.

Bill McDermott describes the moat in one word: **Context**.

ServiceNow says its platform supports roughly 1**00 billion workflows** and nearly **8 trillion transactions**. Amit Zavery said more than **500 customers were live with AI Control Tower** in the first six months. And ServiceNow reported **AI ACV above one billion dollars** in Q2, with a full-year target of $1.5B.

The **CMDB** knows assets, services, owners and dependencies. **ITSM and change management** know how work is routed and approved. **IRM** understands controls, risks, issues and evidence.

A best-of-breed specialist will likely have deeper model analytics, but it often lacks the **operational graph** that identifies the owner, business service or the path to remediate an issue.

The installed base gives ServiceNow a right to compete. It does not, by itself, prove that every technical control is present or every runtime path is governed.

### Field study of fifteen ServiceNow customers

A quick word on methodology.

TheCUBE Research commissioned a study through its partner, Qualitate, which conducted the fieldwork from September 15 through September 21, 2026.

The final base is 15 completed large-enterprise interviews totaling 575 minutes. Eleven respondents were in North America and four in Europe. Five came from financial services, four from healthcare, three from technology and telecommunications, and three from public sector, manufacturing or other industries.

The sample was senior: Three executives or vice presidents, ten directors or functional heads, and two senior managers.

**Every respondent had an existing ServiceNow footprint.** The study is a deliberate qualitative study of expansion, coexistence, implementation and control boundaries inside real accounts. **Eleven of the fifteen customers had either installed, piloted or were actively evaluating ServiceNow AI Control Tower.**

There’s of course a bias toward the ServiceNow installed base. That is by design and it’s useful because management’s premise is it has an installed-base premise. We are testing the environment where Control Tower should have its greatest advantage.

Our methodology specifically separates direct experience from management claims. **This is not a survey with fifteen customers supplied by ServiceNow.**

### ServiceNow is building on its workflow and operational moat

This next chart speaks to the heart of the episode.

**All fifteen respondents recognized ServiceNow’s workflow, operational integration or incumbency advantage.**

Fourteen of fifteen, however described **runtime enforcement** as external, custom, human mediated, limited to selected paths or **not proven at enterprise scale**. The one exception was a limited financial-services pilot that successfully tested ServiceNow’s blocking capability for at least one model and one agent.

Twelve of fifteen identified a **model-specific evidence gap** – validation records, lineage, bias, explainability, drift history or AI-specific regulatory artifacts.

And twelve of fifteen tied governance value or **switching cost** to the wider Now Platform – mainly ITSM, CMDB, change management and SecOps.

Our research shows that **the same ServiceNow architecture creates both the moat and the boundary limits.** Specifically, ServiceNow is hard to displace because governance work is embedded in operations. But **the value story degrades when the CMDB is immature, the AI estate sits outsid

In an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider said […]
content_en:
Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. In an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider said to think of Attie as “social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”

# Bluesky’s AI tool now lets you make games and apps to share on social

Attie launched earlier this year as a way to build your own feeds with AI, but Bluesky is expanding what it can do.

You can make your own Attie app by typing in a prompt. A simple poll I made about *Pokémon Red* and *Pokémon Blue* took a few minutes to generate. If you want to check out something more full-featured, the Attie website currently highlights a few examples like a “Flappy Butterfly” *Flappy Bird* clone, a drum machine, a quiz, and an idle clicker about a celery man, and each has a custom link on the attie.site domain and attribution for who made the social app at the bottom of the page. The apps I’ve messed around with are pretty lightweight novelties, though I liked the drum machine.

content_en:
### IBM ties intelligent operations to agent safety and business value

Intelligent operations begin with a business question: What should artificial intelligence help an enterprise accomplish? As agents take on more work, organizations need an operating model that connects their actions to customer outcomes, infrastructure dependencies and financial accountability.

IBM Corp.’s approach brings automation, data and operational signals into that broader framework. Moving beyond isolated projects requires teams to consider how their work fits across the business, according to Tyler Lynch (pictured), outbound Chief Technology Officer, IBM Automation Portfolio, at IBM.

“First off, instead of just being a developer or whatever that is, take a step back and think about capabilities and outcomes that you want to deliver for your customers and your clients,” they said. “That’s where we should all be starting. It’s going to have multidisciplinary pillars, and that’s what we should all be doing.”

Lynch spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier for IBM’s AI Operating Model interview series, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed agent controls, infrastructure context and measuring AI value ahead of IBM TechXchange 2026. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Extending agent safety to financial risk

Building on IBM’s focus on enterprise AI orchestration and production readiness, agent oversight must account for how people deploy and use these systems. No single approach fits every working environment, Lynch explained.

“We have agents that are deployed that are operating like applications, and some are autonomous, some are not and some are delegated,” they said. “But then we have local agents, what I would consider co-work agents. This could be your coding agent. Those are very different modalities from authorization, logging and telemetry, and no one’s nailed it yet.”

IBM supports Nvidia Corp.’s Open Agent Safety Platform, contributing enterprise capabilities spanning agent identity, credentials and hybrid infrastructure. Lynch’s discussions with the team at Apptio Inc., an IBM company, have also raised questions about extending agent safety into financial oversight.

“We can now start to emit telemetry directly out of these agents for token usage in and out,” they said. “Why can’t we have policies evaluate that just like we do for \[identity threat detection and response\] and maybe revoke an agent’s \[application programming interface\] key so it can stop? Put it in the corner until a human can go look at it.”

### Giving intelligent operations shared infrastructure context

Acting on operational signals also requires understanding the environment an agent might change. HashiCorp Inc.’s Infragraph is now available to eligible Terraform customers on a limited basis.

“Infragraph is a graph-based representation of your infrastructure, but we’re extending that to be more of a knowledge graph,” Lynch said. “It’ll actually be used by our FinOps tools and our observability tools, and they will also enrich that graph.”

Shared infrastructure context could help teams assess changes beyond the resources a particular configuration directly manages. Other applications or users may rely on those resources without the team making the change seeing those dependencies, Lynch explained.

“I like the more complex use cases, which is catching the errors that humans might not catch,” they said. “Dependency impact analysis is something I’m very much interested in as a scientific area. Can we do dependency impact analysis to determine if \[a change\] would adversely affect anybody else?”

### Measuring outcomes beyond token consumption

For intelligent operations, spending alone can’t show whether AI delivers value. Enterprises need to connect that investment to the outcomes of the processes they’re changing, Lynch explained.

“For me, speed of business matters, and that’s really hard to quantify sometimes,” they said. “I talk to people \[asking\], ‘Can we get something to market faster?’ That’s not just software development; that is maybe an underwriting process. It’s not just, ‘Did I fulfill an order?’ It is, ‘Did I do it faster? Did I do it better?’”

The financial operating practices supporting those decisions also develop in stages, moving from retrospective cloud bills toward shorter optimization cycles and forecasting based on actual spending. Those practices can extend operational information to FinOps teams, controllers and chief financial officers. For enterprises preparing for IBM TechXchange, Lynch emphasized thinking beyond individual roles and focusing on customer outcomes.

“How do we inform them all? You can’t do that all on day one,” they said. “We land, and then we expand.”

title: TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
excerpt: TSMC had a record quarter, but it can't make chips for everyone as Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom and AMD fight for capacity.
title_en: TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
excerpt_en: TSMC had a record quarter, but it can't make chips for everyone as Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom and AMD fight for capacity.
content_en:
As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s record quarter makes clear, demand from chipmakers shows no sign of slowing down. In fact, TSMC can't manufacture quickly enough.

The artificial intelligence boom has created unending need for space on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, and it could put a chokehold on the entire industry's ability to scale. Last year, TSMC said it had the capacity to make more than 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. But customers want more.

"The competition is extremely fierce," said Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities. "It's a game of who can get the most leverage and supply."

TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, the graphics processors and central processors from Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom that are necessary for running AI workloads. Now a growing number of tech firms – Apple, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI – also rely on TSMC to make custom in-house AI accelerators.

TSMC North American CEO Sajiv Dalal told CNBC he gets at least 10 calls a day about wafer capacity. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter on Thursday and expects fourth-quarter revenue to be 58% higher than a year earlier, driven by strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies.

If compute demand continues to grow at the current rate over the next 12 to 18 months, Klein said capacity constraints at TSMC could threaten some of the industry's massive infrastructure investments and the "aggressive revenue growth targets" from the AI companies. U.S. hyperscalers are projecting well over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, and analysts expect that figure to jump in 2027.

AI ambitions are also threatened by a global shortage of memory chips. The logic chips that TSMC manufactures are more complex and expensive to produce. That means GPU and CPU leaders like Nvidia and AMD work out lengthy contracts and bespoke deals with TSMC behind closed doors years in advance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su have both visited Taiwan multiple times this year.

Sid Sheth, CEO of AI chip startup D-Matrix, has fostered a relationship with TSMC for more than 20 years, and his company relies on TSMC to manufacture its processors.

For TSMC customers, many roads lead to Kevin Zhang, a senior vice president of the Taiwanese company and a central figure in determining which chipmakers get access to its coveted factory lines.

He's "currently probably the most popular person on the planet," Sheth said in an interview. Sheth said that Jerry Qubain, D-Matrix's vice president of manufacturing, has been visiting TSMC since 1992 and goes to Taiwan three to four times a year.

"This was even before Nvidia was founded," Sheth said. "That's a good example of a person we brought on board because of the relationships he has at TSMC." Qubain joined D-Matrix in 2024. TSMC declined to participate in this story.

## Betting on startups

TSMC had 534 customers in 2025. While it doesn't name or rank them, its top 10 customers accounted for 78% of net revenue, with its top two bringing in 19% and 17%, respectively.

That leaves startups competing for capacity against customers with far bigger orders. Sheth said TSMC is "selective," but has an incentive to back promising newcomers.

"They were very supportive of Nvidia and Broadcom when they were very young companies, and now these are their biggest customers today," Sheth said. "They want to see a repeat of that."

TSMC is hustling to bring much more capacity online, with new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona — it's making advanced chips in the U.S. for the first time. In July, TSMC announced it was adding $100 billion and "several more" fabs to the six planned in Arizona, bringing its total commitment to $265 billion. TSMC is also reportedly considering an entirely new fab location in Texas.

All of this will take years to come online. In the meantime, analysts say TSMC is adding tools like ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to existing factories to ramp up capacity. ASML smashed profit expectations in its earnings report Wednesday and said customers are interested in placing orders through 2030.

TSMC isn't the only option. Capacity constraints create an opening for the other two leading advanced chip manufacturers, Samsung and Intel, to win customers.

"People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Dan Hutcheson, an analyst at TechInsights, told CNBC.

That second source might be Intel, the only U.S.-based advanced logic manufacturer. Although its foundry business has been struggling with delays and setbacks for years, Hutcheson says all the big chipmakers are now testing there.

Trade association SEMI expects 102 new chip fabs will come online globally by 2029, including 15 in the U.S. and 78 in Asia. China is the primary growth engine, expected to nearly triple capacity by 2030. In a race to catch up, American fab investments are projected to more than double by 2029.

With an increasing Arizona presence and "extremely fierce" competition for wafer capacity, Klein says TSMC is "one of the best strategically positioned companies on the face of the planet."
